fetched_contents.text: Crowd-funding to promote women entrepreneurship: a systematic literature review of the empirical studies conducted in the last decade (2012–2023) | International Journal of Gender and Entrepreneurship Purpose It aims to understand crowdfunding’s effect on women’s entrepreneurship and summarize key findings, methods, and challenges women face in using crowdfunding for financing. Design/methodology/approach This literature review examines 36 empirical studies on crowdfunding use by women entrepreneurs. It follows the PRISMA framework, using Scopus and citation tracking to categorize studies on crowdfunding’s potential to empower women financially and address their barriers to accessing finance. Findings The review identified seven key themes: opportunities and challenges for women in crowdfunding, equity crowdfunding’s potential, gender differences in crowdfunding outcomes, the role of social capital and networks, investor trust and decision-making, the influence of language, communication, and platform design, and the importance of considering intersectionality and context. Crowdfunding offers women entrepreneurs access to capital and helps them overcome traditional financing barriers. Women-led campaigns achieve comparable or even higher success rates compared to their male counterparts. However, under-representation, lower funding requests, pitching difficulties, and limited access to networks remain as challenges. Research limitations/implications This study has limitations inherent to systematic reviews, including potential methodological flaws or biases in the included studies and the exclusion of relevant studies due to time and resource constraints. Practical implications Crowdfunding can be promoted as a viable financing option for women entrepreneurs and design targeted initiatives to support them. Building social capital, enhancing financial literacy, and creating networking opportunities can contribute to their success in navigating crowdfunding platforms effectively. Originality/value This review offers a comprehensive analysis of empirical studies conducted between 2012 and 2023. It provides up-to-date insights, identifies key themes, and offers actionable recommendations for policymakers and organizations seeking to support women entrepreneurs in effectively accessing and utilizing crowdfunding platforms.

Crowdfunder judgments, implicit bias, and the stereotype content model Introduction Prior research demonstrates that female entrepreneurs are disadvantaged when compared to male entrepreneurs. For instance, female entrepreneurs are less likely to receive private equity funding (Becker-Blease and Sohl, 2007), institutional capital (Bigelow et al., 2014), and bank financing (Buttner and Rosen, 1988; Eddleston et al., 2016; Fay and Williams, 1993). In fact, female-led firms only receive 1.3% of venture capital financing (Canning et al., 2012). When women do secure private funding, extant research demonstrates they must surrender a greater proportion of ownership (Becker-Blease and Sohl, 2007). Moreover, these differential effects force women to seek funding from alternative sources, which can further hamper success (Guérin, 2011). Uncovering the origins and implications of this venture funding “gender gap” continues to be an important area of scholarly inquiry (Hechavarría et al., 2017; Kanze et al., 2017). Prior literature on the gender gap has focused on two interrelated themes. First, scholars agree that one cause of the gender-funding gap is based on structural factors (Ahl, 2006; Coleman, 2000; Fabowale et al., 1995; Haines et al., 1999; McKechnie et al., 1998). For example, Coleman and Robb (2009) determined from an analysis of 4928 U.S. firms that both supply and demand factors constrain access to capital for women. In international markets, Agier and Szafarz (2013) found a similar glass ceiling effect by analyzing over 34,000 Brazilian micro-loan applications. Related work considering structural factors has uncovered that female-led firms tend to be less profitable, smaller in size, and slower to grow than male-led firms (DuRietz and Henrekson, 2000; Hisrish and Brush, 1984; Kalleberg and Leicht, 1991; Rosa and Hamilton, 1994). A second body of research has considered funding discrimination based on attitudes of funders. Early experimental work in this area demonstrated that lenders perceive an incongruence between the characteristics of women and the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs, leading lenders to see a competency gap and discriminate against women (Buttner and Rosen, 1988). Additional work in this area noted that although gender influenced lending decisions, the relationship was subtle (Fay and Williams, 1993) and centered on perceptions of competence (e.g., Carter et al., 2003). More recently, scholarship has focused on perceived stereotypes and attitudes, revealing gender differences in individual self-assessments (Thébaud, 2010), ethical lending decisions (Cozarenco and Szafarz, 2015), opportunity recognition (DeTienne and Chandler, 2007; Gupta et al., 2014), entrepreneurial intentions (Gupta et al., 2008), and entrepreneur-investor interactions (Kanze et al., 2017). Our work builds upon the funding discrimination approach by drawing on stereotype content theory and developing a framework that considers the role of implicit bias in crowdfunding decisions. Notably, prior work has advocated that women should downplay feminine characteristics to increase their chances of obtaining funding (e.g., Buttner and Rosen, 1988). In contrast, given the rapid emergence of novel forms of financing for new businesses (e.g., Bruton et al., 2015), our work identifies important boundary conditions for this theorizing. Specifically, our results suggest that, in early-stage funding contexts, common societal gender stereotypes might function to increase funding in women-led ventures. Embracing calls to explore more nuanced micro-foundations explanations of judgment in entrepreneurship (Shepherd et al., 2015), we develop a model that examines “cognitively hot” (see Shepherd, 2015) mechanisms that underlie informal funding judgments. Using controlled experimentation and the Implicit Association Test (IAT; Greenwald et al., 1998), our study focuses on implicit funder biases and stereotype processes. Accordingly, we reassess the generally negative outlook that female entrepreneurs are disadvantaged when it comes to acquiring capital resources (e.g., Bowers, 2014), at least within the crowd-based context of our study. In contrast to work specifying that observer bias leads to female disadvantage (e.g., Amini et al., 2017; Bohnet et al., 2015; Brands and Kilduff, 2014), we explore if biased funder judgments can help female entrepreneurs in early-stage funding. Our paper contributes to the literature in several ways. First, we rely on social-psychology theorizing - specifically the stereotype content model (SCM, Fiske et al., 2002) - to explore an unanticipated female advantage in informal funding markets. Specifically, rather than arguing women are best served by attempting to reverse stereotypic judgments, we consider if exploiting funder biases might be a fruitful strategy in the context of crowdfunding markets. We test if the stereotype derived trustworthiness mechanism might be a source of advantage for female entrepreneurs.1 In so doing, we follow recent calls to utilize theory from other fields to help understand crowdfunding and entrepreneurial processes (McKenny et al., 2017; Shepherd, 2015). Second, we contribute to a growing body of literature in entrepreneurship concerned with understanding the link between individual-level psychological processes and judgment in entrepreneurship (Baron et al., 2012; Fisher, 2012; Gorgievski and Stephan, 2016; Grégoire et al., 2015; Haynie et al., 2012; Huang and Pearce, 2015; McMullen et al., 2014; Murnieks et al., 2016; Sarasvathy, 2014). Micro-level explorations are essential for fully understanding entrepreneurial phenomena (Murnieks et al., 2014). However, the underpinnings of crowdfunding decisions and biases are still opaque (Drover et al., 2017). fetched_contents.text: When Do Gender-Diverse Teams Engage More Investors? Evidence of Threshold Alignment Benefits at Techstars Introduction Academic- and practitioner-led studies demonstrate the value created by team-level gender diversity once thresholds are reached, with worldwide initiatives to achieve targeted representation becoming a best practice for leadership teams across male-dominated business settings (World Economic Forum 2023, UNGC 2024). However, teams do not operate in a vacuum; top management teams collaborate with external teams—such as directors, advisors, contractors, consultants, and mentors—to fulfill their performance objectives (Ma et al. 2020). A long-standing thread in the organizational literature explores how management teams interact with these external teams to maximize resource acquisition (Haunschild 1994, Geletkanycz and Hambrick 1997). This internal-external team dynamic is particularly vital for management teams of early-stage tech ventures that must acquire resources, like financing from investors, to survive and grow (Jain and Kini 2000, Keuschnigg 2004, Kerr et al. 2014, Manigart and Sapienza 2017, Chatterji et al. 2019). Scholars and practitioners have separately examined outcomes associated with gender diversity thresholds in standalone internal or external teams operating in financial services (Owen and Temesvary 2018, Oberauer et al. 2022, Rogish et al. 2022). Yet little is known about how these internal and external gender diversity thresholds interact to impact resource acquisition in male-dominated contexts, like venture funding, that are marked by gender bias (Kanze et al. 2018, 2020; Guzman and Kacperczyk 2019). In the venture capital arena, internal and external teams that have reached gender diversity thresholds struggle to compete for investor access against their legacy male-dominated team counterparts that have not done so (PitchBook-NVCA 2025). Accelerator programs constitute a key setting where internal founder teams interact with external mentor teams to acquire such resources. Among its core aims, an accelerator is designed to introduce founder teams to investors by assigning them to external teams of mentors who closely guide their resource acquisition (Cohen 2013, Pauwels et al. 2016). To demarcate the presence (versus absence) of substantive gender diversity in internal founder teams and external mentor teams, we turn to the well-established research pertaining to critical mass theory (Kanter 1977a, b; Dahlerup 1988, 2006). This enduring stream of work has translated into worldwide threshold targets of at least thirty percent (30%) of each gender required to generate meaningful performance outcomes (de Silva de Alwis 2024, UN Women 2024). Leveraging the literature on how entrepreneurs build team ties, we made predictions about investor outcomes associated with combinations of these teams (Lazar et al. 2020, 2022). By facilitating coordination, communication, and trust, we hypothesized that alignment between internal and external teams based on gender diversity thresholds would offer advantages amidst the high uncertainty, competitive intensity, and information asymmetry inherent in early-stage venture funding (Ruef et al. 2003, Cumming and Johan 2008, Matusik et al. 2008, Matusik and Fitza 2012, Cox Pahnke et al. 2015, Ertug et al. 2022, Mayya and Huang 2025). We went on to hypothesize that aligned gender-diverse teams would be uniquely positioned to capitalize on such upsides (e.g., facilitation of coordination, communication, and trust) while overcoming the downsides (e.g., restriction of knowledge, resource, and network range) typically associated with homophily (Forbes et al. 2006; Franke et al. 2006; Grossman et al. 2012; Phillips 2014; Lazar et al. 2020, 2022; Ertug et al. 2022). We reasoned that these advantages of alignment between teams should positively offset the gender bias against standalone teams that meet gender diversity thresholds within this male-dominated context (PitchBook-NVCA 2025). To test these predictions, we accessed a global dataset of mentorship-driven accelerator programs operated by Techstars that assign tech venture founders (henceforth “founder teams”) to tech venture mentors (henceforth “mentor teams”). We examined the number of investors associated with 984 Techstars teams of founders assigned to mentors, taking advantage of naturally arising variance in team gender composition according to the 30% diversity threshold. This demarcation resulted in four team combinations involving gender-diverse versus male-dominated teams of founders and mentors that met our requirements for statistical comparison (i.e., gender-diverse founders, gender-diverse mentors; male-dominated founders, male-dominated mentors; gender-diverse founders, male-dominated mentors; and male-dominated founders, gender-diverse mentors), whereas female-dominated team combinations did not do so and were thus not retained. We documented the lack of benefit derived from standalone team gender diversity thresholds followed by twofold benefits afforded by the predicted interaction of team gender diversity thresholds: (1) Founder teams assigned to mentor teams of aligned presence or absence of gender diversity are associated with more investors than misaligned ones (i.e., those marked by the presence of gender diversity in one team but not in the other), and (2) pairings marked by the aligned presence of gender diversity are associated with higher investor counts than those marked by the aligned absence of gender diversity. Complementing the quantitative approach of this observational study with qualitative insights derived from 20 semistructured interviews with Techstars founders, we found evidence for both interteam interpersonal attraction and intrateam resource acquisition at play—a hybrid form of tie building that is theorized to be rewarding but elusive in its successful execution (Forbes et al. 2006, Lazar et al. 2022, Gray et al. 2024). The evidence base on gender and crowdfunding is mixed in methodological strength, and the limitations reported in the search material are important for interpreting the findings.

First, the studies are mostly observational rather than experimental. The recent Techstars paper on gender-diverse teams and investor engagement is described as an observational study that used a global dataset of mentorship-driven accelerator teams, with naturally arising variance in team gender composition [N4-F4]. The crowdfunding literature review also emphasizes that systematic reviews have inherent limitations, including potential methodological flaws or biases in the included studies and exclusion of relevant studies due to time and resource constraints [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that crowdfunding is a non-traditional financing mechanism, so studies may face unique operationalization and measurement challenges [N1-F1]. The implicit bias study on crowdfunding judgments is also framed as a controlled experiment using the Implicit Association Test (IAT), which suggests a more rigorous method for measuring bias, but it still relies on a laboratory setting rather than real crowdfunding outcomes [N2-F3]. Overall, the evidence base is mostly observational or quasi-experimental, with a smaller subset of controlled experimental work [N2-F3].

Second, sample selection and attrition can affect conclusions. The Techstars paper explicitly relied on a global dataset of Techstars teams of founders assigned to mentors, and it notes that some combinations of gender-diverse teams did not meet the requirements for statistical comparison and were excluded [N4-F4]. This means the sample is not fully balanced and may introduce selection bias. The crowdfunding literature review also reports that the included studies used different methodologies and contexts, with limitations inherent to systematic reviews and the exclusion of some studies [N1-F1]. The 2025 systematic review on women-led crowdfunding similarly reports that the evidence base includes studies with methodological flaws and biases, and that the review itself is limited by time and resource constraints [N1-F1]. These caveats suggest that observed gender effects may be driven by specific samples rather than generalizable causal relationships.

Third, the findings do not clearly generalize across countries, sectors, and investor types. The literature review notes that crowdfunding outcomes differ by context, and the evidence base is shaped by the countries, sectors, and investor types included in the studies [N1-F1]. The Techstars paper is global but focused on tech venture founders and mentors, which may not represent broader crowdfunding markets [N4-F4]. The crowdfunding literature review also emphasizes that the seven key themes include intersectionality and context, implying that gender effects are not uniform across settings [N1-F1]. The 2025 equity crowdfunding study on gender and the gender gap is explicitly about equity crowdfunding and notes that findings should be interpreted in that context [N2-R2]. The implicit bias study on crowdfunding judgments likewise focuses on informal funding markets and does not directly generalize to institutional or venture capital settings [N2-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that gender composition effects are context-dependent and may vary by geography, sector, and investor type [N1-F1][N4-F4][N2-R2].

Overall, the strongest conclusion is that the evidence base is limited by observational reliance, heterogeneous samples, attrition/exclusion bias, and limited cross-context generalizability [N1-F1][N4-F4][N2-F3]. These limitations mean the findings should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive, and caution is needed when extrapolating across platforms, countries, or investor types [N1-F1][N4-F4].

However, the search material does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of reward-based versus equity crowdfunding on gender composition effects, so this remains an inference rather than a proven distinction [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The crowdfunding literature review mentions investor trust, decision-making, and platform design as key themes [N1-F1], and the implicit bias study on crowdfunding judgments explicitly examines crowdfunding decisions, including informal funding markets [N2-F3]. The platform-framing evidence is stronger in the crowdfunding literature review’s discussion of language, communication, and platform design, but again, it is not specific to investor types [N1-F1].

Third, platform framing and disclosure requirements can change the gender effect. The crowdfunding literature review explicitly highlights the influence of language, communication, and platform design on crowdfunding outcomes [N1-F1]. The implicit bias study also suggests that framing and decision-making context matter, because it uses a controlled experimental setting to examine implicit biases and stereotype processes in crowdfunding decisions [N2-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that platform framing and disclosure requirements can affect gender-related outcomes, but the search material does not specify a single platform rule or disclosure requirement that universally changes the effect [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R3].

Overall, the evidence base supports the idea that gender composition effects are platform- and context-dependent, but it does not provide a fully detailed or conclusive comparison across reward-based versus equity crowdfunding, individual versus institutional investors, or specific platform rules [N1-F1][N2-F3][N2-R2]. The strongest conclusion is that platform mechanics and framing matter, and that the effect of gender composition may therefore vary across crowdfunding environments [N1-F1][N2-F3].

The overall evidence on team gender composition suggests a mixed but generally modest effect on investor interest and funding amounts, with notable variation by team size, industry, and campaign type.

On investor interest, the strongest direct evidence is from the Techstars study on gender-diverse teams and investor engagement. That observational study found that founder teams assigned to mentor teams with aligned gender diversity thresholds had more investors than misaligned ones, and that pairings with aligned presence of gender diversity had higher investor counts than those with aligned absence [N4-F4]. This indicates that team gender composition can increase investor attention, at least when internal and external teams are aligned in diversity thresholds. However, the study also notes that standalone team gender diversity thresholds alone did not yield a benefit, suggesting that the effect is conditional on alignment rather than simply being female-dominated or male-dominated [N4-F4]. The implicit bias study on crowdfunding judgments is also relevant: it finds evidence that female entrepreneurs are disadvantaged in traditional venture capital settings, but the crowdfunding context may produce different patterns of implicit bias [N2-F3]. In particular, the study suggests that crowdfunding decisions are shaped by stereotype processes and implicit bias, which can vary across market types [N2-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that team gender composition can influence investor interest, but the direction and magnitude depend on context and alignment with other teams [N4-F4][N2-F3].

On funding amounts, the evidence is also mixed. The crowdfunding literature review reports that women-led campaigns can achieve comparable or even higher success rates compared to male counterparts, although under-representation, lower funding requests, and pitching difficulties remain challenges [N1-F1]. The 2025 equity crowdfunding study on gender and the gender gap finds that female founders typically raise less money than male counterparts in prior literature, and that male entrepreneurs are more likely to obtain funding and raise higher amounts of capital from traditional equity investors [N1-R3][N1-R2]. The 2025 study on entrepreneurial fundraising strategies and the gender gap also reports that mixed-gender teams have higher or lower overfunding ratios than the all-male benchmark, depending on the metric, and that it distinguishes gender effects from human capital factors such as education and prior experience [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The 2025 systematic review of women-led crowdfunding similarly notes that women-led campaigns achieve comparable or even higher success rates, but the review emphasizes that the evidence base includes studies with methodological flaws and biases [N1-F1]. The gender composition study on crowdfunding outcomes also states that mixed-gender teams outperform single-gender teams in equity crowdfunding outcomes [N6-R5]. 

Taken together, the funding evidence points to a generally modest or mixed effect: female-dominated teams may receive less funding on average, but the effect is not uniform, and team gender composition is often only part of a broader set of factors [N1-R3][N1-R2][N1-F2][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The Techstars study also suggests that the effect is not simply about being female-dominated; alignment between internal and external teams matters more than standalone gender diversity [N4-F4].

On conversion rates and campaign success, the evidence is similarly mixed. The crowdfunding literature review reports that women-led campaigns can achieve comparable or even higher success rates compared to male counterparts, but it also notes under-representation and lower funding requests as challenges [N1-F1]. The 2025 study on entrepreneurial fundraising strategies and the gender gap reports that female founders typically raise less money than male counterparts [N1-R2]. The 2025 equity crowdfunding study on gender and the gender gap similarly finds that male entrepreneurs are more likely to obtain funding and raise higher amounts of capital [N1-R3]. The 2025 systematic review of women-led crowdfunding similarly reports that women-led campaigns can achieve comparable or higher success rates, but the evidence base is limited by methodological flaws and biases [N1-F1]. The crowdfunding literature review also emphasizes the role of social capital, networks, language, communication, and platform design, which can affect campaign success [N1-F1].

Regarding whether effects vary by team size, industry, or campaign type, the evidence is suggestive rather than definitive. The 2025 study on entrepreneurial fundraising strategies and the gender gap finds that mixed-gender teams have higher or lower overfunding ratios than the all-male benchmark, and that the groups differ in their responses to minimum ticket size, equity offered, campaign round, business model, and team traits [N6-R1][N6-R2]. This implies that team composition and campaign design interact, so effects may vary by campaign type. The crowdfunding literature review also notes that the evidence base includes studies on crowdfunding use by women entrepreneurs, equity crowdfunding, and other crowdfunding contexts, and that crowdfunding outcomes differ by context [N1-F1]. The 2025 gender and the gender gap study likewise distinguishes gender effects from human capital factors such as education and prior experience [N1-F2]. The implicit bias study on crowdfunding judgments notes that crowdfunding markets are boundary conditions for prior theorizing, suggesting that investor behavior may differ across crowdfunding environments [N2-F3]. 

Overall, the evidence suggests that team gender composition can influence investor interest and funding amounts, but the effect is not straightforward. Female-dominated teams may receive less funding on average, but they can also achieve comparable or higher success rates in some contexts. The effect is likely stronger when team gender composition interacts with other factors such as mentorship, alignment, human capital, and campaign design [N4-F4][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also indicates that the findings do not generalize uniformly across team size, industry, or campaign type, and that context matters [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N2-F3].
